* Install a single receptacle at the designated location, with conduit piped down the wall to provide a protected wiring method.

This dedicated circuit will provide a separate power source for the radon fan rather than relying on a shared circuit serving other basement equipment and receptacles.

2. Dedicated 20-Amp Exercise Area Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit to supply the basement exercise area.
* Install three receptacles to accommodate the designated exercise equipment.
* Install two receptacles along the wall bordering the mechanical room.
* Reuse the existing conduit at the designated location, remove the existing receptacle wiring, and install new wiring and a new receptacle.

Providing a dedicated circuit for the exercise area will help accommodate the electrical demand of the equipment without adding additional loads to the general basement receptacle circuit.

3. Dedicated 20-Amp Basement Kitchenette Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit to supply the planned basement kitchenette.
* Install two receptacle locations at the designated areas.
* Pick up the upstairs kitchen island receptacle as part of this circuit using wiring accessible from the basement.

Including the upstairs kitchen island receptacle on this new circuit will help remove its load from the existing circuit serving the basement lighting, screened-in porch, and existing exterior receptacles. This will help distribute the electrical demand more appropriately and reduce the likelihood of nuisance tripping on the existing circuit.

This circuit will provide a separate power source for the kitchenette and kitchen island receptacles, helping distribute the electrical load as the basement living space is developed.

4. Dedicated 20-Amp Fireplace Heater Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit dedicated to the basement fireplace heater.
* Install one receptacle at the designated location, with conduit piped down the wall.

A dedicated circuit will help accommodate the heater’s electrical demand without unnecessarily loading the general-purpose basement receptacle circuit.

5. Dedicated 20-Amp Exterior Hot Tub Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit from the basement subpanel, routed across the basement and drilled through the exterior wall to the back porch.
* Install one weather-resistant GFCI receptacle with an appropriate in-use bubble cover to supply the 120-volt inflatable hot tub.

Because this receptacle will serve equipment used around water, proper ground-fault protection is particularly important. GFCI protection is designed to quickly interrupt power when an electrical fault creates a potentially dangerous shock hazard.

The final circuit and receptacle arrangement will need to meet the hot tub manufacturer’s electrical requirements and applicable code requirements for the installation location.

6. Dedicated 20-Amp General Basement Receptacle Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit to supply the remaining designated basement receptacles.
* Reuse the existing conduit at one location and install a new receptacle.
* Cut in one receptacle along the stairway wall.
* Install three additional receptacles at the designated locations, using conduit down the block walls as needed.

This additional circuit will provide convenient receptacle access throughout the basement while distributing the electrical demand across multiple circuits instead of continuing to rely on the existing overloaded arrangement.

Basement Circuit Protection

The six new circuits will be installed from the existing basement subpanel using the appropriate wiring methods and circuit protection for their intended applications. The estimate includes:

* Four 20-amp dual-function AFCI/GFCI circuit breakers.
* One 20-amp AFCI circuit breaker.
* One 15-amp AFCI circuit breaker.

AFCI protection is designed to detect certain dangerous electrical arcing conditions that can lead to fires. GFCI protection helps reduce the risk of electrical shock by detecting ground faults and interrupting power. Dual-function breakers combine both protective features in one device.

The specified breakers will provide the intended protection for the new circuits while helping bring the installation into compliance with applicable electrical code requirements.

Existing Basement Wiring – Junction Box Transition

Currently, one existing circuit supplies the basement lighting and receptacles, exterior receptacles, screened-in porch receptacles, and kitchen island receptacle. This places a substantial number of electrical loads on a single circuit and can contribute to nuisance tripping when multiple devices are operating.

As part of this project, LPH will disconnect and transition the existing basement wiring as necessary, installing accessible junction boxes along the basement ceiling to maintain continuity for the existing circuits. This will allow the existing wiring to remain operational while the new circuits take over the designated basement receptacle loads and the upstairs kitchen island receptacle is transferred to the new kitchenette circuit.

The goal is to distribute the electrical demand more appropriately, reduce the burden on the existing circuit, and provide a more functional electrical layout for the basement and the home’s connected areas.

Whole-Home Surge Protection Recommendation

With the installation of multiple new circuits and sensitive AFCI/GFCI protective devices, LPH recommends adding a whole-home surge protector at the main electrical panel.

Modern electrical equipment, appliances, and electronic circuit boards can be damaged by voltage surges originating from utility disturbances, lightning-related events, or electrical equipment cycling on and off within the home. These events can also contribute to premature wear or damage to sensitive electronic components.

A whole-home surge protector provides an additional layer of defense by helping divert damaging transient voltage away from the home’s electrical system and connected equipment. It is particularly beneficial for homes with modern appliances, HVAC equipment, electronics, and other sensitive devices.

Although surge protection cannot prevent every type of electrical disturbance or guarantee that equipment will never be damaged, it is a worthwhile protective upgrade for the home.

Additional 20-Amp Exterior Circuit From the Main Panel

LPH will install one additional 20-amp circuit from the main electrical panel to supply two receptacles serving the main garage area: one receptacle inside the garage below the electrical panel and one exterior receptacle on the opposite side of the wall.

This installation will include:

* Routing the new circuit from the main panel and dropping down the wall to the designated locations.
* Installing a GFCI-protected receptacle at the designated exterior location.
* Installing one receptacle inside the garage below the electrical panel.
* Providing convenient power sources for both interior garage and exterior use.
* Providing a more suitable power source for the garage microwave, reducing reliance on the existing garage door opener receptacle and extension cord.

Currently, the microwave is being powered through the garage door opener receptacle using an extension cord. This is not an ideal arrangement for an appliance that draws substantial current, particularly when the circuit may already be supplying other equipment. A properly installed receptacle on a new circuit will provide a more appropriate power source and help reduce nuisance tripping caused by shared electrical loads.

Exterior Receptacle Repairs and Weather Protection

LPH will also address the damaged exterior receptacles by replacing the existing devices with new weather-resistant receptacles and providing the required GFCI protection.

This portion of the work includes:

* Two weather-resistant GFCI receptacles.
* Two weather-resistant duplex receptacles.
* Reuse of the existing boxes and appropriate bubble covers where suitable.

Weather-resistant receptacles are designed to better withstand outdoor environmental exposure. Combined with appropriate GFCI protection and suitable covers, these replacements will help reduce the risk of moisture-related deterioration, electrical faults, and shock hazards.

The existing boxes are already equipped with appropriate bubble covers, so the existing covers will be retained where they are in suitable condition and compatible with the new receptacles.

Additional Grounding and Bonding Improvements

LPH recommends completing the home’s grounding and bonding system by installing a grounding clamp on the existing metal water line and adding approximately 5 feet of grounding conductor to bond the home’s gas piping system as required by applicable electrical code.

* Water Line Grounding: Install an approved grounding clamp on the existing metal water line and connect it to the home’s grounding electrode system as appropriate. This will address the incomplete grounding arrangement and help establish the required electrical connection to the metal water piping where applicable.
* Gas Line Bonding: Install approximately 5 feet of additional grounding conductor to properly bond the home’s gas piping system to the electrical grounding system, as required by applicable code provisions.

Proper grounding and bonding help provide a safe, intentional path for fault current, allowing protective devices to operate as intended during an electrical fault. These connections also help reduce dangerous voltage differences between metal piping systems and other grounded electrical components.

Completing these improvements will help bring the home’s grounding and bonding system into compliance with applicable electrical code requirements and provide an additional layer of protection for the home’s occupants and electrical equipment.

Installation, Testing, and Completion

All new circuits will be routed from the designated electrical panels using appropriate wiring methods, conduit, junction boxes, and circuit protection for their intended applications. LPH will complete the installation in accordance with applicable electrical code requirements, verify the new connections, and test the installed devices and circuits for proper operation.

The overall goal of this project is to provide a safer, more organized, and more functional electrical system for the unfinished basement and surrounding areas. By adding dedicated circuits for the radon fan, exercise equipment, kitchenette, fireplace heater, and hot tub, transferring the upstairs kitchen island receptacle to the new kitchenette circuit, expanding general receptacle capacity, and addressing the exterior electrical concerns, LPH will help accommodate the home’s electrical needs while reducing dependence on the existing heavily loaded circuit.

e.345090633:
LPH recommends replacing the existing 34-year-old Crouse-Hinds electrical panel with a brand-new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel while retaining the home’s existing 200-amp service capacity.

Although the existing Crouse-Hinds panel is rated for 200 amps, its age and original design make replacement a worthwhile investment in the home’s electrical safety, reliability, and ability to accommodate modern electrical demands. Electrical panels are responsible for distributing power throughout the home and providing overcurrent protection to individual circuits. As panels age, breakers and internal connection points can experience wear, deterioration, and reduced reliability. Breaker connections on the bus bar can also loosen over time, potentially causing overheating, arcing, or unreliable circuit operation.

Why Upgrade the Existing Panel?

1. Aging Electrical Equipment

At approximately 34 years old, the existing Crouse-Hinds panel has provided decades of service. However, its age warrants consideration of replacement before deterioration or component failures create a more urgent situation. Replacing the panel allows LPH to install new equipment rather than continuing to depend on aging internal components and connections.

2. Better Support for Today’s Electrical Demands

Modern homes typically place greater demands on their electrical systems than they did decades ago. Today’s households rely on larger appliances, home office equipment, entertainment systems, exercise equipment, electronic devices, and other electrical loads that may not have been anticipated when the original panel was installed.

The existing panel’s 200-amp rating does not automatically mean the home needs a larger service. However, replacing the older panel provides an opportunity to improve circuit organization, evaluate the home’s electrical distribution, and accommodate additional circuit protection and future electrical projects where capacity permits.

3. Upgrade to a New 42-Space Eaton CH Panel

LPH will replace the existing Crouse-Hinds panel with a new 42-space Eaton CH panel. This provides a modern panel assembly with additional circuit spaces to help organize the home’s electrical system and accommodate future circuit additions, subject to the available service and load capacity.

The new panel will also provide a suitable platform for compatible circuit breakers and modern protective devices as needed for the home’s electrical requirements.

4. Improved Long-Term Reliability and Serviceability

Replacing the existing panel allows LPH to evaluate the incoming service conductors, grounding and bonding connections, neutral and ground terminations, and branch-circuit connections as part of the installation. This includes inspecting the breaker connections at the bus bar for looseness, signs of overheating, or other conditions that may affect safe operation. This helps identify concerns that may otherwise remain hidden within aging equipment.

A new panel can also make future electrical maintenance and troubleshooting more straightforward by providing current, compatible equipment and a more organized circuit layout.

5. Opportunity to Incorporate Whole-Home Surge Protection

As part of the panel replacement, LPH recommends installing whole-home surge protection to help protect sensitive electronics and appliances from damaging voltage transients originating from utility disturbances, lightning-related events, and electrical equipment cycling within the home.

Modern appliances and electronic equipment contain circuit boards and sensitive components that can be vulnerable to voltage surges. Whole-home surge protection provides an additional layer of defense for the home’s electrical system and connected equipment.

Scope of Work

LPH will:

* Remove the existing 34-year-old Crouse-Hinds electrical panel.
* Install a new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel while maintaining the existing 200-amp service rating, provided the existing service components and installation support that configuration.
* Transfer the existing branch circuits to the new panel using compatible circuit breakers and appropriate wiring methods.
* Inspect breaker connections at the bus bar and address any loose, damaged, or overheated connections identified during the installation.
* Inspect and address grounding, bonding, neutral, and equipment grounding connections as required for the installation.
* Verify circuit identification and organize the panel directory.
* Evaluate the existing service connections and associated components for any additional concerns identified during replacement.
* Test the completed installation to verify proper operation.
* Provide whole-home surge protection as a recommended additional upgrade, if included in the approved scope.

The Long-Term Benefit

Replacing the existing Crouse-Hinds panel is a proactive investment in the home’s electrical infrastructure. Rather than waiting for aging equipment to develop a problem, the homeowner can move forward with a modern panel that offers additional circuit spaces, improved serviceability, and a better foundation for future electrical upgrades.

The goal is not simply to replace a panel because it is old. It is to update an aging, critical electrical component so the home’s distribution system is better positioned to serve the family’s current needs and future electrical demands.

* inducer has been leaking inside the furnace

* rust on burners
* igniter is oxidized

e.344497301:
200 Amp Underground Electrical Service Replacement

Reason for Replacement

The existing electrical service equipment has deteriorated significantly due to age, prolonged electrical loading, and the demands placed on the home’s electrical system. The main electrical panel is completely full, and the subpanel is also nearly at capacity, leaving limited room for additional circuits while placing continued demands on the existing equipment.

The homeowner has reported noticeable voltage drops when new electrical loads begin drawing power. During the electrical evaluation, LPH tightened the panel connections; however, when pressure was applied to the service cable wiring, electrical arcing could still be heard, and some circuits were observed experiencing intermittent operation.

These conditions are serious warning signs that the existing service connections and electrical distribution equipment may have deteriorated to the point where reliable electrical contact can no longer be assured. Loose or deteriorated connections can generate excessive heat and electrical arcing, potentially damaging equipment and increasing the risk of electrical failure or fire.

Due to the combination of noticeable voltage fluctuations, audible electrical arcing, intermittent circuit operation, deteriorated equipment, and heavily loaded panels, LPH recommends replacing the existing electrical service rather than continuing to rely on aging components. Simply tightening connections or replacing individual breakers would not adequately address the overall condition of the existing service equipment.

A complete service replacement will provide new service equipment, updated electrical distribution, improved circuit capacity, and a modernized grounding and bonding system to help restore reliable power delivery and reduce the risks associated with the deteriorated installation.

Scope of Work: 200 Amp Underground Electrical Service Upgrade

LPH will modernize the home’s electrical service by replacing the existing service equipment with a new 200 Amp system, including a new exterior emergency disconnect and a new interior electrical panel.

Scope of Work Includes:

* Remove the existing deteriorated electrical panel and associated service equipment.
* Install a new 200 Amp meter base.
* Replace the underground service entrance conductors and associated connections as required by the approved scope and utility requirements.
* Install a new exterior 200 Amp emergency disconnect to provide an accessible means of shutting off power to the home during an emergency or when servicing the electrical system.
* Install a new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel.
* Transfer and properly terminate existing branch circuits in the new panel.
* Install new breakers throughout the panel as required for the existing circuits.
* Properly separate neutral and grounding conductors within the new panel.
* Upgrade the grounding and bonding system to meet applicable electrical code requirements.
* Install top-tier whole-home surge protection at the new electrical panel.
* Install protective conduit for exterior service conductors where applicable to protect against physical damage and environmental exposure.
* Properly seal applicable service entry points to help prevent moisture intrusion.
* Label the new electrical panel and individual circuits.
* Inspect and verify electrical connections, terminations, grounding, and bonding.
* Coordinate required permits, inspections, and PPL scheduling as applicable.
* Test the completed installation and verify proper operation of the electrical system.

Why a Complete Replacement Is Recommended

1. Addressing Electrical Arcing and Intermittent Power

Audible arcing when pressure is applied to the service cable wiring, combined with circuits intermittently going in and out, indicates a potentially hazardous connection or equipment failure. Electrical arcing can produce intense localized heat, damage conductors and terminals, and increase the risk of an electrical fire. These conditions warrant prompt corrective action.

2. Correcting Voltage Fluctuations Under Load

Noticeable voltage drops when new electrical loads start can indicate excessive voltage drop, deteriorated connections, inadequate conductors, or another supply-side or distribution problem. A complete service replacement will allow the affected service components and connections to be replaced, although the underlying cause of the voltage fluctuations must be verified rather than assumed.

3. Replacing Deteriorated Electrical Equipment

The existing equipment has experienced decades of service and prolonged electrical loading. Aging breakers, bus connections, and terminations can deteriorate over time. Replacing the existing panel and service equipment will establish a new foundation for dependable electrical distribution rather than continuing to rely on components showing signs of deterioration.

4. Improving Electrical Capacity and Organization

The main panel is completely full, and the subpanel is nearly full. The new 42-space Eaton CH panel will provide additional circuit spaces and a modernized distribution arrangement. The new 200 Amp service will also provide greater capacity where supported by the home’s calculated electrical load and the utility service.

5. Adding an Exterior Emergency Disconnect

The new exterior emergency disconnect will provide an accessible means of disconnecting power to the home. This improves accessibility for emergency response and servicing while modernizing the home’s service equipment.

6. Protecting Connected Electronics and Appliances

The new whole-home surge protective device will help protect sensitive electronics, appliances, and other connected equipment from damaging voltage surges caused by lightning, utility disturbances, and other electrical events.

Underground Service Protection and Longevity

The new service equipment will be installed with appropriate protection and sealing to help minimize exposure to physical damage and moisture intrusion. Exterior service conductors will be installed in protective conduit where applicable to the installation and utility requirements.

Replacing the service connections, meter base, exterior emergency disconnect, and interior electrical panel will address the major components included in this service replacement and help establish a more reliable electrical infrastructure for the home.

Peace-of-Mind Warranty

The new Eaton CH electrical panel and breakers are protected by a 10-year parts and labor warranty while the homeowner maintains an active LPH Service Partner Plan (SPP) membership, providing continued coverage and additional peace of mind.

Long-Term Value

This project is more than a routine electrical panel replacement. It addresses documented concerns involving voltage fluctuations, audible arcing, intermittent circuit operation, aging service equipment, and limited panel capacity.

By replacing the existing service equipment, installing a new exterior emergency disconnect, upgrading grounding and bonding, and adding whole-home surge protection, LPH will help address the conditions affecting the home’s electrical reliability while providing a modernized 200 Amp electrical service designed to support the home’s needs for years to come.

All work will be completed in accordance with applicable electrical code requirements and the requirements of the serving utility and local authority having jurisdiction.

i.340612653:
Electrical System Check Summary

LPH performed an electrical system evaluation throughout the home to assess the condition and operation of the electrical system, identify potential safety concerns, and verify proper operation where accessible. During the evaluation, LPH reviewed the electrical panel and circuit protection, checked for visible signs of deterioration or overheating, inspected accessible wiring and connections, and performed electrical testing to evaluate proper voltage and breaker operation.

Electrical Panel and Arc-Fault Breaker Findings

During the inspection, LPH noticed light carbon dust deposits near the Eaton BR-style dual-function arc-fault breakers inside the electrical panel. To verify proper operation, LPH began testing the breakers using an appropriate circuit tester. The initial breaker tested failed to trip as intended, prompting LPH to test every arc-fault breaker in the panel.

During this process, seven 20-amp Eaton BR-style dual-function arc-fault breakers failed. Two breakers visibly sparked through their clear test buttons and experienced internal component failure, producing an immediate burnt odor. The remaining five breakers made loud electrical noises consistent with coil chattering before failing.

These failures indicate that the affected breakers have experienced internal component malfunctions and can no longer be relied upon to provide their intended circuit protection. Since these devices are designed to protect electrical circuits from dangerous fault conditions, leaving failed breakers in service creates a safety concern and may increase the risk of electrical overheating or fire.

LPH performed additional voltage testing to confirm proper voltage and evaluate the overall stability of the electrical system. The remainder of the system tested stable at the time of evaluation. Based on the testing performed, the breaker failures appear to be an isolated anomaly rather than an indication of a system-wide electrical problem. However, the exact cause of the failures has not been confirmed.

Receptacle and Switch Wiring Evaluation

LPH also identified that the home’s receptacles and switches were wired using the stab-back method, in which conductors are inserted into push-in terminals on the devices rather than secured under the side-terminal screws. Although this wiring method is commonly found in residential properties, these connections can become less reliable over time and may be more susceptible to loosening or developing poor electrical contact under certain conditions.

LPH opened accessible electrical boxes to inspect the wiring and connections. No loose connections were identified during the inspection. While no immediate connection issues were found, LPH will continue to monitor the condition of these connections during the home’s yearly electrical system checks to identify any developing concerns and recommend corrective action if necessary.

Recommended Corrective Action and Customer Approval

LPH recommended the immediate replacement of all seven failed 20-amp Eaton BR-style dual-function arc-fault breakers. The approved scope of work includes:

* Removing the seven failed arc-fault breakers.
* Supplying and installing seven new, compatible 20-amp Eaton BR-style dual-function arc-fault breakers.
* Inspecting accessible breaker connections and affected panel areas for signs of heat damage or deterioration.
* Verifying proper voltage and testing the affected circuits following installation to confirm proper operation.

The homeowner has approved the recommended work. Due to a time constraint with the homeowner’s appointment, the down payment and scheduling arrangements will need to be completed following the conclusion of this call.

Because this is a pressing electrical safety concern, LPH will make every effort to schedule the approved work as soon as possible.

Today’s invoice and electrical evaluation will be emailed to the homeowner for their records.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home. We appreciate the opportunity to address this electrical safety concern and look forward to completing the necessary repairs as soon as possible.

e.343982375:
Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 16 grains per gallon. A hardness level of 16 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, shower heads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a cabinet water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water heater to allow for efficient integration into the home’s main water distribution system. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located behind the washer connecting to the washer drain. Technician will have to open up the drywall. at the proposed installation area. The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. An outlet is provided. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

A water softener reduces hard minerals—primarily calcium and magnesium—in your home's water. If you have hard water, installing one can make a noticeable difference in cleaning, bathing, and maintaining your plumbing and appliances.
Top 7 benefits of a water softener
1. Less limescale buildup
Helps prevent the white, chalky deposits that form on faucets, showerheads, glass shower doors, and inside pipes and water-using appliances.
2. Softer-feeling skin and hair
Many people find their skin feels less dry and their hair feels easier to manage because soap rinses away more easily. A softener does not treat skin conditions, however.
3. Cleaner dishes and glassware
Reduces mineral spots, cloudy glassware, and residue left behind after washing.
4. Softer laundry
Clothes and towels may feel less stiff, and you can often use less laundry detergent because soft water allows soap to work more effectively.
5. Longer-lasting appliances
Helps limit mineral scale in water heaters, dishwashers, washing machines, and other equipment, potentially improving efficiency and reducing maintenance.
6. Less cleaning and scrubbing
Spend less time removing hard-water rings, crusty faucet deposits, and soap scum from sinks, tubs, and showers.
7. Potential savings over time
Reduced scale buildup, lower soap consumption, and fewer mineral-related repairs can help offset the cost of the system.

i.341115614: This morning I arrived at the Radanovic family home to perfrom their annual electrical system and safety check. Upon my arrival Mr. Radanovic informed me he only wanted me to check his main service. I found only one discrepancy which was a shared neutral in the sub panel. Two separate circuits using one neutral can lead to an overload of the neutral. This overloading can cause damage, burning, or loss of neutral connection. IF this neutral were to lose its connection, the two circuits remaining energized could overload with no exit path and become potentially 240v circuits, destroying any appliances or equipment not rated to handle that much voltage. I have provided an option to replace these two circuits with an appropriate double pole breaker. That is my only recommendation for today. If you have any questions or concerns please do not hesitate to reach out. Thank you.

During the evaluation, we inspected the electrical service, panel, circuit breakers, accessible wiring and connections, receptacles, switches, grounding and bonding, GFCI protection, smoke and carbon monoxide detection, and accessible interior and exterior electrical devices. We looked for signs of corrosion, moisture intrusion, physical damage, deteriorated components, loose connections, improper installations, and other potential electrical safety concerns.

During today’s evaluation, several receptacles were found to have deteriorated due to moisture exposure, corrosion, and physical damage. The following options were presented to the homeowner to address these concerns and improve the home’s electrical safety.

Approved Work Completed:

* Basement Receptacles: Replaced two existing receptacles with new weather-resistant GFCI receptacles. One existing device had suffered extensive corrosion due to moisture entering through the block walls, while the other had sustained physical damage that caused the face of the receptacle to break apart.

Water had entered the electrical box and soaked the receptacle, leaving the device and screw terminals in a state of significant deterioration. LPH installed a new weather-resistant GFCI receptacle along with a proper in-use weatherproof cover to provide protection against moisture exposure while the receptacle is being used.
* Smoke Detector Installation: Installed five new battery-operated smoke detectors equipped with sealed 10-year lithium batteries throughout the home.
* Combination Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detector: Installed one new battery-operated combination smoke and carbon monoxide detector equipped with a sealed 10-year lithium battery in the upstairs hallway to provide early warning of potential fire and carbon monoxide hazards.

e.346069605:
A water softener removes the minerals that make water “hard,” mainly calcium and magnesium. These minerals are naturally found in groundwater and can cause buildup on faucets, inside pipes, and in water-using appliances.
 1. Less white scale and mineral buildup
Helps prevent chalky deposits on faucets, showerheads, glass shower doors, and inside pipes and water heaters. Existing buildup may still need cleaning.
2. Soap and shampoo work better
Soft water makes it easier to create a lather, reduces soap scum, and can leave skin feeling less dry or tight after bathing.
3. Easier cleaning around the house
You may spend less time scrubbing white spots off sinks, tubs, shower walls, and fixtures.
4. Helps protect appliances
Reducing scale can help water heaters, dishwashers, washing machines, and other water-using equipment operate more efficiently and potentially last longer.
5. Softer-feeling laundry
Clothes and towels may feel less stiff, and fabrics may accumulate less mineral residue.
6. Can reduce plumbing maintenance
By limiting new scale formation, a softener can help prevent mineral deposits from narrowing pipes and clogging fixtures.
7. Potential savings on cleaning products
Because soap and detergent work more effectively in soft water, you may be able to use less of them, depending on the product and your water hardness.

i.341545395: This morning I arrived at the Harrison family home for their annual electrical system and safety check. Upon performing a thorough evaluation of the homes main electrical service I found no major discrepancies. However, Mrs. Harrison informed me that they have had a history of blowing the fuses that supply power to their hot water heater. After performing an analysis of the system I noted several things. First, and most importantly, I noted that the wire which supplies power to the disconnect is undersized. The water heater requires a 30A (amp) supply in order to properly function. The wire which is currently in use is only rated AT MOST to handle 20A. The heater, the disconnect itself, and the breaker are all designed for a 30A load, where as the wiring, which acts as the bridge for all of these systems is only designed for 20A. Secondly, the Harrisons have been using 20A replacement fuses for this 30A system which is why they have been blowing with such frequency. Unfortunately, stepping the fuses up to 30A could become a potential fire hazard with the wire unable to handle that load. If 30A fuses are installed, that wire may burn and become damaged well before that fuse would ever blow. I have some indication of potential heat as it seems the ends of the stripped insulation on the hot wires has begun to soften and partially deform. I encouraged the Harrisons to continue to use these 20A fuses until they are able to replace the system. While they may blow more frequently, it is all that can be done until we replace the wiring, which is imperative. I have provided two options. The first which is most recommended would consist of replace the disconnect with a modern electrical disconnect requiring no fuses, and to replace the wire. The second option would be to replace the wire solely to avoid potential overheating. If you have any questions or if you would like to move forward with these options, please do not hesitate to reach out. Thank you, and we will see you in our next visit!

e.344030245: LPH will replace undersized fused disconnect and its subsequent undersized wire with appropriate 10AWG 30A rated wiring and non-fused disconnect.

LPH arrived at the residence to perform a thorough electrical system check evaluation. During the evaluation, we reviewed the electrical panel and breakers, inspected for signs of overheating and deterioration, discussed whole-home surge protection, and evaluated the exterior receptacles for proper weather protection and safe operation. We also discussed the installation of customer-supplied exterior light fixtures.

During the inspection, LPH identified three older-style Cutler-Hammer arc-fault breakers exhibiting excessive heat buildup and extensive carbon dust accumulation on the electrical panel cover. These conditions may indicate deterioration of the breakers and warrant replacement to help restore reliable circuit protection and reduce the risk of continued overheating.

We also discussed the benefits of installing whole-home surge protection at the main electrical service. Transient voltage spikes can occur from utility fluctuations, lightning activity, and the everyday operation of electrical equipment throughout the home. Over time, these voltage fluctuations can contribute to premature wear of sensitive electronic components in appliances, LED lighting drivers, and other household electronics. The homeowner has experienced premature LED bulb failures and flickering throughout the home. Although these symptoms can have multiple causes, whole-home surge protection provides an added layer of defense against damaging voltage surges and helps protect the home’s electrical devices and appliances.

Additionally, LPH identified the need to replace the rear porch receptacle with a weather-resistant GFCI receptacle and an extra-duty, in-use bubble cover. The existing cover cannot close while the awning remains plugged in, leaving the receptacle vulnerable to moisture and water intrusion. The recommended replacement will provide protection from the elements while the awning is connected, helping reduce the risk of corrosion, nuisance tripping, and premature receptacle failure.

All findings and recommended options were thoroughly reviewed with the homeowner, including the replacement of the three arc-fault breakers, installation of whole-home surge protection, replacement of the rear porch receptacle and protective cover, and installation of the homeowner-supplied exterior light fixtures.

The homeowner elected to move forward with all recommended options. The work has been scheduled for November 9th, and a down payment was collected.

e.344408722:
Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection
LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.
Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:
	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.

Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 5 grains per gallon (GPG) and the chlorine level to be . 5 ppm. A hardness level of 5 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, shower heads , and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water heater. The water softener inlet would come from the water meter approximately 20’ away. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located near the water meter. The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. The home’s electrical panel is located approximately 20 feet away, and an outlet will need to be installed and provided at the equipment location prior to or as part of the installation. i.341685691:
This estimate includes having Lancaster Plumbing and Heating make a warranty repair on the water softener. It would include removal of the mechanical parts of the head that control the stages of the water softeners regeneration. This repair is covered under both the manufacturer’s parts warranty and Lancaster Plumbing and Heating’s labor warranty.

We came out today to take a look at the water softener because it was showing an error code. The error code was indicating that there was a motor failure. This usually means that during regeneration the computer was telling the spacer stack assembly to switch positions and it took too long or got stuck.

The technician began diagnosing the issue by disconnecting power and trying a hard reset of the electrical components. This did not fix the issue, so the technician provided an estimate to perform a warranty repair. The warranty repair included replacing the spacer stack assembly, and the motor that drives the functions for the spacer stack assembly. Once the repair was completed, the technician put the water softener through an abbreviated regeneration twice in order to verify that the system was now working properly. Both attempts on the abbreviated regeneration were successful and everything was in proper operation at this time.

The technician did discover a secondary issue, but it had to do with the Brian tank. LPH completed a heating system inspection on a 10-year-old Trane gas furnace. At this time, all system components are operating properly.

During the inspection, LPH observed that the blower wheel was slightly dirty and noted potential microbial growth in the supply plenum. LPH also found that the blower motor capacitor was slightly out of specification.

Recommendations:
LPH recommends performing a furnace cleaning to remove buildup from the blower wheel and clean the supply plenum. LPH also recommends replacing the blower motor capacitor to help maintain proper system operation and reduce the risk of unexpected breakdowns.

Performing these preventative maintenance services can help improve airflow, support system efficiency, and reduce the risk of premature component failure. If microbial growth is confirmed, appropriate cleaning and treatment should be performed as needed.

LPH also discussed indoor air quality (IAQ) package options with the homeowner and provided available options for consideration. The homeowner respectfully declined the recommended services at this time.

We began our evaluation at the main electrical/distribution panel. This is where we assessed the internal conditions, age, connections and voltage readings. During this inspection, most of the inspected parameters meet the required threshold for a healthy panel. However, there are a few recommendations we assessed during this inspection. 

First we discovered that these panels are the Zinsco brand, which is a brand that lost their UL listing many years ago and is no longer allowed to be installed. This brand along, with two other brands that have similar issues, no longer have any replacement parts or breakers available. Second we noticed that this electrical system is currently within the “end of life” range, which means the longevity is in question. Lastly, there’s no system put in place to protect appliances/electronics from spikes of electric which target the sensitive components inside these units. A whole home surge protection device is recommended if the homeowners were interested in  protecting their main utility equipment with a one time investment unit.

Next, we inspected all of the protective systems for personnel and equipment in the home such as the smoke detectors, GFI protection devices, and the grounding system. First, we discovered that the water meter does not meet today’s grounding standards to protect against any leakage of electricity from traveling on the pipes. The next was identifying that all of the existing smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors are either not currently installed or past their 10 year lifespan. Lastly, we identified multiple areas with missing GFI protection, which is the bathroom, the washer in the basement, kitchen and exterior. All other devices in the home were tested and functioning properly prior to leaving today.

The existing 1.5 HP submersible well pump is approximately 20 years old. Technician recommends replacing the existing pump with a new 2 HP submersible well pump to provide the appropriate pumping capacity for the depth of the well. A 2 HP submersible well pump is rated for well depths up to approximately 900 feet. The existing pump is currently set at approximately 760 feet, and the total well depth is approximately 935 feet.

Due to the depth of the well and the pump setting, 1” galvanized well pipe is required instead of 1” poly well pipe. Technician recommends replacing the existing 20-year-old galvanized well pipe and well wire along with the new well pump. Replacing these components will provide new piping and wiring throughout the well and help eliminate potential issues associated with the age of the existing components.

The existing well control box is also approximately 20 years old. Technician recommends replacing the control box with the new pump to ensure the electrical components are properly matched to the new 2 HP pump. Technician also recommends replacing the existing pressure tank and tank tee assembly. The new tank assembly would include a 40/60 pressure switch, pressure gauge, pressure relief valve, and drain-down valve. Replacing these components at the same time will provide a complete upgrade of the well system’s pumping and pressure-control components.

Gas pressure was not able to be adjusted at the gas valve when locked into low and high fire, therefore I recommend replacing the entire gas valve as the over feeding is a problem both for safety and efficiency of the unit.

We were called out to provide options to remedy any power loss concern for Evan and his family. Upon arrival, we spoke with Evan, who informed us of what exactly he was looking for in portable generators systems, and wanted some clarity on some information that he researched on his own time. After speaking with Evan, we got a great understanding of what he was looking for to be installed in this home and for length of the time that he planned on staying in this home. We were looking to install a new 50 amp plug on the exterior of the home with a twist lock style receptacle, a new 50 amp breaker that will be protected and controlled by an interlock kit that will fit this panel cover exactly. We also looked at the outdoor unit to assess the amperage/wattage usage and noticed that it will work with the two generators that Evan was looking into(8,500W or 11,000W). However, we did inform Evan that if he went with the 8.5 KW style generator, he would be very limited in total usage after the outdoor unit, freezer, and well pump were under use.

Evan also had a question/concern with his water pipe for his water heater, and if it needed to be properly grounded/bonded. We informed Evan that the equipment grounding conductor, feeding this water heater is acting as the main grounding source and bonding it by other means would be more on the redundant side than actual productive dispersion side. If Evan still wanted a separate ground wire installed from the main panel to the water heater location, we could take care of that. However, it is not needed by national electric code standards, per NEC 250.104(B). 

The options provided and invoice for today’s visits will be emailed to Evan for his record and to review. We thank you for allowing us into your home and we look forward to servicing you in the future.

i.342391384: This afternoon I arrived at the Mitchell family home to conduct their annual electrical system and safety check. Upon my arrival, Mr. Mitchell informed me of some concerns related to the location of his breaker panel. Upon performing an inspection I found the breaker panel to be located in the downstairs bathroom. According to NEC revision 1993, breaker panels are not allowed to be located in any bathroom facilities, The code defines a bathroom (Article 100) as any area including a basin (sink) with one or more fixtures like a toilet, tub, or shower. Even a half-bath or powder room with just a sink and a toilet legally meets this definition. Therefore, overcurrent devices and service panels are still forbidden under NEC 240.24(E). For this reason, I have built the Mitchell’s an option to relocate their main electrical panel to a separate location in the basement outside the bathroom, and away from other water piping related systems. Otherwise I presented several other estimates regarding some code compliance features in the home. Ultimately I found the main electrical systems to be in goof physical condition with no signs of deterioration. If you have any questions or concerns related to todays visit, please do not hesitate to reach out! Thank you for having us out today and I look forward to our next visit!

Due to its age and deteriorated condition, I recommend replacing the main electrical panel to help ensure the safety and reliability of the home’s electrical system. I also found that the switch controlling the lamppost was beginning to fail. I informed the homeowner that replacing the GFCI outlet and the failing switch would help restore proper functionality to both fixtures.

Recommendations:

* Replace the main electrical panel due to its age, significant rust, and poor condition.

i.342862190:
Technician investigated concerns of sewer gas odor entering the main-floor master bathroom shower area and laundry room. Technician checked the water level in the master bathroom shower drain and inspected the 3” vent termination through the roof, which is located directly above the master bathroom. The 3” vent was found to extend approximately 6–8” above the roof.

Technician explained that windy conditions can create a Venturi effect at the vent termination, potentially drawing air through the vent system and affecting the water seal in the shower P-trap. Wind can also create direct downdrafts through the vent, which may contribute to sewer gas odors entering the home. Technician discussed raising the existing vent termination and adding a U-bend configuration using two 3” 90° fittings to help reduce the potential for wind-driven downdrafts.

Technician also recommended installing a 2” Trap Guard in the shower drain. The Trap Guard allows water to drain normally while providing an additional barrier to help prevent sewer gas from entering the home if the P-trap water seal is compromised.

The main-floor laundry room is equipped with two laundry drains, each with a 2” P-trap. One of the drains is not regularly used, and the water in the P-trap may be evaporating and allowing sewer gas to enter the laundry room. The unused drain will either be used for the dehumidifier discharge to maintain the P-trap water seal or capped to prevent sewer gas from entering through the drain.

The homeowner plans to purchase a trap guard before addressing the vent through the roof.

Next, we inspected all of the protective systems for personnel and equipment in the home such as the smoke detectors, GFI protection devices, and the grounding system. First, we discovered that the water meter does meet today’s grounding standards to protect against any leakage of electricity from traveling on the pipes. The next was confirmation that all of the existing smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors are installed in the right locations and up-to-date. Lastly, we identified two areas with missing GFI protection, which is the bathroom and for the washer in the basement. All other devices in the home were tested and functioning properly prior to leaving today.

We provided options to remedy all of our electrical recommendations, which was presented today. The basic electrical package was approved and completed today. We installed all new GFI protection for both exterior receptacles, GFI receptacles on the first floor, and for the bathroom/washer receptacle in the basement. All receptacles were to the homeowners approval and tested and working properly prior to leaving today. However, we had to adjust the box in the basement bathroom/laundry area, which involved an open section of drywall that we cannot repair. We sealed this area up with white silicone and took $50 off the total job to satisfy this issue. All of the options that were not approved will be emailed along with the electrical evaluation form and invoice for today’s visit. Exterior Receptacle Replacement

LPH will replace three exterior receptacles that are not rated for outdoor use. During the evaluation, visible corrosion was found inside the receptacles, along with rust on the mounting screws, indicating moisture intrusion over time. Two of these receptacles are exposed to direct rainfall and currently have standard gray covers that do not provide adequate protection when water reaches the devices.

To help prevent further moisture damage and improve protection against the outdoor elements, LPH will replace all three receptacles with weather-resistant devices. The two existing gray covers will be upgraded to extra-duty, weatherproof in-use bubble covers, which are designed to provide protection while cords remain plugged in. All associated electrical boxes will be properly resealed to help prevent additional water intrusion.

Why this matters: Exterior receptacles are continually exposed to changing weather conditions, and moisture can accelerate corrosion, compromise electrical connections, and increase the risk of electrical faults. These upgrades will provide improved protection against rain and moisture while helping extend the service life of the receptacles.

Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection
LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.
Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:
	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.
	• Can help extend the service life of modern appliances and equipment by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.
	• Helps minimize the likelihood of costly repairs or premature equipment replacement due to surge damage.
	• Provides continuous protection for the entire home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
	• Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.
As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

Premium Surge Protection Warranty & Replacement Coverage

The installed surge protection device also provides additional protection beyond the device itself. If the surge protector is ever sacrificed or fails as a result of a covered surge event, the device is backed by a lifetime warranty and coverage of up to $100,000 toward covered damage to the home’s electrical components and connected equipment, subject to the manufacturer’s warranty terms and conditions.

If the surge protector ever needs to be replaced under the warranty, the replacement device is provided at no charge. LPH will also handle the replacement installation for a $150 labor charge, helping make future warranty replacement straightforward and affordable for the homeowner.

This means the homeowner is not simply purchasing a surge protector—they are adding a long-term layer of protection to the home’s electrical system while also having manufacturer-backed coverage in the event of a significant surge.

As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

A Moen Flo is a smart water monitoring and leak-detection system for your home. It’s designed to help prevent expensive water damage from leaking pipes, broken hoses, running toilets, or burst plumbing.
What does a Moen Flo do?
1. Detects leaks
Monitors the water flowing through your home's main water line.
Learns your household's normal water-use patterns.
Can detect unusual water flow that may indicate a leak.
2. Automatically shuts off your water
If it detects a serious leak or abnormal water use, it can automatically turn off your home's main water supply to help prevent flooding.
You can also shut the water off remotely using the app, depending on your setup.
3. Monitors water usage
Shows how much water your household uses.
Can help identify unusual usage, such as a toilet that keeps running.
4. Sends alerts to your phone
- Notifies you about possible leaks, unusual water use, and other problems.
Moen says its system can detect some leaks as small as one drop per minute. It needs to be properly installed and configured, and it isn't a guarantee against all water damage.

Technician performed a thorough plumbing system inspection on all accessible plumbing fixtures throughout the home to evaluate overall operation, drainage, water flow, and visible plumbing conditions. e.344279558:
The trip lever/tub stopper in the 2nd-floor hallway bathroom bathtub is not functioning because the existing lever is broken. The bathtub is equipped with a PVC Watco waste and overflow assembly. Technician recommends replacing the broken trip lever with a new PVC Watco trip lever compatible with the existing waste and overflow assembly. This will restore proper operation of the bathtub stopper, allowing the stopper to open and close as intended for filling and draining the bathtub.

The existing second-floor hallway bathroom toilet is a standard-height, round-bowl toilet that is older and outdated. Technician recommends replacing the existing toilet with a new comfort-height, elongated-bowl toilet. The comfort-height design provides added comfort and ease of use, while the elongated bowl offers additional seating space. The new toilet will also use less water per flush, helping improve water efficiency and reduce overall water consumption. Technician will remove the existing toilet, install the new toilet with a new wax ring and supply connection as needed, and test the toilet to ensure proper flushing, filling, and operation with no leaks.

During the annual plumbing system check, Technician noticed that the main-floor kitchen sink drain gurgles when draining. Technician inspected the kitchen sink drainage system and found that the drain is not properly vented. Improper venting can restrict airflow within the drainage system, causing gurgling noises and potentially affecting the drain’s ability to discharge wastewater properly. Technician recommends installing an air admittance valve (AAV) on the kitchen sink drain to provide the necessary airflow and help maintain proper drainage. This will help equalize pressure within the drain piping, reduce gurgling noises, and allow wastewater to drain more efficiently. Technician will install the air admittance valve in an accessible location and test the kitchen sink drain to verify proper operation.

During the plumbing system inspection, Technician noticed that the existing sump pump pit is not equipped with a sump pump. Water was present inside the pit, indicating that groundwater is entering the sump pit and that the basement may be susceptible to groundwater accumulation and potential flooding. Technician recommends installing a new sump pump in the existing pit to help remove accumulated groundwater and reduce the risk of basement flooding and potential water damage.

The sump pump discharge piping would be installed to direct water from the pump to the exterior of the home. The discharge line would terminate approximately 25 feet away at the rear of the house, running along the basement stairwell and extending beyond the end of the stairwell to direct water away from the foundation. A designated electrical outlet would need to be provided to supply power to the new sump pump. Once installed, Technician will test the sump pump and discharge system to verify proper operation and confirm that water is being pumped away from the home.

We came out today because of a leak leak and back up at the food waste disposer. Upon arrival, the homeowners explained what was going on when they discovered the issue which allowed the technician quickly determine what the issue was. The technician discovered that the locking collar for the equipment was not locked in place, and in addition determined that that side of the double bay sink was backed up. 

After further discussion, the technician learned that there were certain things going into the disposer that shouldn’t have been. We also learned that too much food was going down at one time. An estimate was provided to take apart the center drain outlet in order to clear the blockage. Upon disassembling the drain, we did discover a large quantity of food between the first section of drain piping and the second fitting that attaches to the P-trap. We were able to quickly get the blockage clear and the drain piping reassembled. Once everything was back together, the technician tested everything to ensure there were zero leaks and proper flow.

We did provide an estimate to install a customer supplied food waste disposer and to also replace the center drain outlet piping. We are not saying that there needs to be an immediate replacement. This would be a preventative maintenance replacement due to the amount of rust we saw at the locking collar. We also don’t know the condition of the rubber gasket that creates a water tight seal. At this time, everything was in proper operation and leak free.

If you have any other questions or concerns that arise after today’s visit, please do not hesitate to give us a call. Thank you for continuing to trust Lancaster Plumbing and Heating with all of your home service needs.

i.343985425:
LPH arrived to begin the annual electrical system check. Upon arrival, no electrical concerns/questions were reported prior to our electrical inspection. 

We began our evaluation at the main electrical/distribution panel. This is where we assessed the internal conditions, age, connections and voltage readings. During this inspection, all of the inspected parameters meet the required threshold for a healthy panel.

We discovered that there’s no system put in place to protect appliances/electronics from spikes of electric which target the sensitive components inside these units. A whole home surge protection device is recommended if the homeowners were interested in  protecting their main utility equipment with a one time investment unit.

Next, we inspected all of the protective systems for personnel and equipment in the home such as the smoke detectors, GFI protection devices, and the grounding system. First, we discovered that the water meter doe meet today’s grounding standards but the gas piping does not. This grounding system is designed to protect against any leakage of electricity from traveling on the pipes. The next was identifying that the existing smoke detectors are either expired or missing. Lastly, we identified that the front exterior receptacle is no longer secured to the wall. All other devices in the home were tested and functioning properly prior to leaving today.

We provided options to remedy all of our electrical recommendations, which was presented today. All of the options that were not approved will be emailed along with the electrical evaluation form and invoice for today’s visit. We thank you for allowing us in your home to service you and we look forward to servicing you in the future.

e.344275829:
When flushing the toilet in the main floor hallway bathroom, a gurgling sound can be heard coming from the bathtub drain. This may indicate an issue with the existing drain and venting configuration. Upon inspection, the existing bathtub drain consists of 1-1/2” copper piping connected to an S-trap configuration, which is not properly vented and can interfere with the drainage system’s ability to maintain proper airflow. When the toilet is flushed, the sudden discharge of water through the drainage system can create pressure fluctuations that may cause air to be pulled through the bathtub trap, resulting in the gurgling sound. Improper venting can also affect the bathtub trap seal, potentially allowing sewer gases to enter the home if the water seal is compromised. The home’s main plumbing vent is supplied from the top of the main waste stack.

Technician recommends replacing the existing 1-1/2” copper bathtub drain piping with 2” PVC piping and replacing the corroded brass bathtub waste and overflow assembly. This will provide updated drain piping and a new waste and overflow assembly while allowing the existing drain configuration to be evaluated and corrected as needed. Technician will assess the existing S-trap arrangement and determine the appropriate corrections to improve drainage and provide proper venting in accordance with applicable plumbing code requirements.

Technician also recommends inspecting the plumbing vent through the roof to check for possible obstructions, such as debris or other blockages, that could restrict airflow through the vent system. A restricted vent can contribute to gurgling sounds, slow drainage, and improper pressure balance within the plumbing system. Clearing any obstructions found may help restore proper airflow. These recommended repairs and inspections are intended to improve drainage performance, reduce the gurgling sound when flushing the toilet, and help maintain the proper water seal in the bathtub drain trap. Additional venting modifications may be necessary depending on the existing plumbing configuration and the findings during the repair.

e.345022885:
Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 19 grains per gallon (GPG) and the chlorine level to be 1.0 ppm. A hardness level of 19 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, showerheads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water heater to allow for efficient integration into the home’s main water distribution system. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located behind the water heater at the proposed installation area. An outlet is provided. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

i.344256914:
LPH arrived at the residence to perform a comprehensive electrical system check evaluation throughout the home. During the evaluation, LPH inspected the main electrical panel and accessible electrical components, checked breakers and visible connections for signs of deterioration, overheating, corrosion, and improper installation, and evaluated the condition of accessible receptacles, switches, lighting devices, and other electrical components throughout the home. LPH also checked accessible GFCI protection, exterior receptacles and weatherproof covers, and visible wiring conditions for potential safety concerns.

Main Electrical Panel: The existing 42-year-old Crouse-Hinds electrical panel was evaluated and found to have several concerning conditions. Rust was observed on multiple breakers, along with heat discoloration above the main breaker. The original breakers were also noticeably loose, and when gently moved, audible electrical arcing could be heard. These conditions raise concerns regarding deteriorated breaker connections, potential overheating, and the reliability of the existing electrical equipment. Due to the age of the panel and the observed deterioration, LPH discussed replacing the existing panel with a new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel and installing new compatible breakers to improve the safety and reliability of the home’s electrical distribution system.

Basement Circuit: LPH discussed the existing 20-amp basement circuit, where the wiring method involves conductors inserted into the back of the receptacle devices. These connections are beginning to loosen, raising concerns about maintaining reliable electrical contact. Loose electrical connections can create resistance, heat buildup, and potential arcing. LPH reviewed the benefits of correcting these connections using an appropriate wiring and termination method.

GFCI Protection Throughout the Home: LPH evaluated GFCI protection in applicable areas throughout the residence and discussed locations where protection is incomplete, including portions of the kitchen. Proper GFCI protection helps reduce the risk of electrical shock in areas where receptacles may be exposed to moisture or where electrical equipment is used near water. Available options for improving protection in the applicable areas were discussed with the homeowner.

Upstairs Electrical Devices: Several electrical devices upstairs were identified as deteriorated and in need of replacement. The homeowner acknowledged these conditions and stated that addressing the interior device replacements would be part of a future project that they could handle independently.

Attic Above the Garage: LPH identified a live tap box in the attic above the garage. This electrical connection point was discussed with the homeowner as an item requiring attention to ensure the wiring and enclosure are properly installed, protected, and maintained in accordance with applicable electrical code requirements.

Exterior Receptacles: LPH evaluated the accessible exterior receptacles and discussed the need for appropriate GFCI protection and suitable weatherproof covers for the remaining exterior devices. Proper outdoor-rated receptacles and covers help protect electrical connections from moisture and environmental exposure while reducing the potential for corrosion, electrical failure, and shock hazards.

All findings and recommendations were reviewed with the homeowner, including the primary concern involving the deteriorated Crouse-Hinds electrical panel and the additional items identified throughout the home. The homeowner stated that the interior device replacements were something they could address as part of a future project and requested estimates for the electrical panel replacement and the recommended exterior receptacle improvements.

The requested estimates, along with today’s electrical system check evaluation, will be emailed to the homeowner for review and consideration.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home. We appreciate the opportunity to evaluate your electrical system and look forward to servicing you again in the future.
